module_intro: Every concept covered so far describes what to look for on a chart. This module adds when to look for it. ICT-focused teaching treats the 24-hour trading day as sharply uneven in significance, with specific, recurring windows tied to the world's major financial centers carrying far more analytical weight than the hours in between. Works through the daily cycle in order: Asian session/range, London session and its Judas Swing pattern, London Close's quieter continuation behavior, and New York's role in confirming or reversing what came before. Exact clock-time boundaries for each named Kill Zone vary meaningfully (sometimes by 1-3 hours) across ICT-focused secondary sources; this variance is documented explicitly rather than presented as a single false consensus.
prerequisites_stated_in_text: Builds on Market Structure (Module 3), Liquidity (Module 4), and Displacement (Module 5).
module_objectives: explain why ICT-focused teaching treats certain hours of the trading day as more significant than others
mark an Asian Range from a simple price sequence and label its high and low as candidate liquidity pools
describe the full Judas Swing sequence (sweep, displacement, structure shift, FVG entry) associated with the London Open Kill Zone
state the specific invalidation rule used to distinguish a genuine Judas Swing from an actual breakout
explain why New York session price action should be read in light of what the Asian and London sessions already established, rather than in isolation
describe, in general terms, what a trader following this framework should be doing (observing, marking, watching, or acting) during each of the four named Kill Zones

concepts.name: Time & Price Theory
concepts.definition: Time and Price Theory is the foundational ICT principle that price behavior is not uniform throughout the trading day - specific, recurring windows of time are treated as far more likely than others to contain the significant, institutionally driven price delivery that this book's earlier modules (structure, liquidity, displacement) describe.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
ICT-focused teaching, credited throughout to Michael J. Huddleston, treats "time" as a variable of equal or greater importance than "price" alone - the reasoning given across sources is that the same chart pattern (a liquidity sweep, a Fair Value Gap, a Market Structure Shift) is considered meaningfully more reliable when it occurs inside a specific, recurring time window than when the identical pattern occurs outside of it.

This principle is the direct justification for the concept of the Kill Zone, developed through the remainder of this module: specific, named time windows, generally tied to the opening or overlap of major global trading centers (Asia/Tokyo, London, New York), during which institutional participation and therefore tradeable displacement are expected to concentrate.

Sources describe this framework as originally built around observed patterns across the American, Asian, and two European trading windows, explicitly noting that the calmer Pacific/Sydney session was not included among ICT's originally highlighted high-volatility windows.
concepts.beginner_explanation: Financial markets like the forex market trade nearly continuously, 24 hours a day across different countries. But just because a market is technically open does not mean equally significant activity is happening at every hour. Time and Price Theory is the idea that certain hours of the day - tied to when major financial centers like London or New York are opening for business - are simply more important to watch than others, because that is when the largest, most consequential trading activity tends to occur.
detection_criteria: Note the current time in New York (Eastern Time), the reference zone ICT-focused sources consistently recommend anchoring to, regardless of the trader's own physical location.
Cross-reference this time against the specific named Kill Zones developed later in this module (Asian, London Open, London Close, New York Open).
Treat chart activity occurring inside one of these windows as a higher-priority candidate for analysis than identical-looking activity occurring well outside all of them.

Remain aware that all specific Kill Zone boundaries shift by one hour whenever the US or UK individually transitions between standard and daylight saving time, since the two do not always change on the same calendar date.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
An identical-looking Fair Value Gap and Market Structure Shift form at 3:00 AM ET (inside the London Open window) versus at 6:00 PM ET (outside all named windows)

Under Time and Price Theory, the 3:00 AM occurrence would be treated as a materially higher-confidence setup than the 6:00 PM occurrence, purely due to timing - even though the two price patterns, examined on a chart with the time axis hidden, might look identical.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
Time and Price Theory tells the trader when to concentrate analytical attention and, for those trading actively, when to seek entries - treating the 24-hour trading day as unevenly weighted rather than uniform.

It does not tell the trader that significant moves cannot occur outside these windows, nor that every occurrence of a pattern inside a window will succeed. It is a probability-weighting principle, not an exclusionary rule.
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: This concept is the reasoning underneath every specific Kill Zone defined in this module, and is the direct conceptual ancestor of the Power of 3 (Accumulation - Manipulation - Distribution) framework covered in the next module, which maps this same time-based thinking onto a repeatable daily cycle.

framework_placement.comes_before: Requires familiarity with Liquidity (Module 4) and Displacement (Module 5), the specific phenomena this theory claims are time-concentrated.
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds directly into every session and Kill Zone concept in the remainder of this module.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Ignoring time zone and daylight saving adjustments, leading to analysis performed at the wrong actual clock time relative to the intended window.
Treating time-based filtering as a guarantee of a valid setup rather than one input among the many covered throughout this book.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: Time and Price Theory is a widely used organizing principle within ICT-focused teaching, but it is also one of the more externally debated aspects of the method. Some critics, cited even within ICT-focused secondary sources themselves, note that modern trading is heavily automated and that significant news-driven volatility can occur at any hour, regardless of named session windows - this book presents Time and Price Theory as ICT-focused teaching describes it, while noting this open point of debate.
dependencies: the specific phenomena this theory claims are time-concentrated

concepts.name: Asian Session
concepts.definition: The Asian session is the trading period during which Asia-Pacific financial centers (principally Tokyo, alongside Sydney) are active, generally treated by ICT-focused sources as the first major session of the daily trading cycle and typically characterized by comparatively lower volatility and volume relative to the London and New York sessions.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
ICT-focused sources consistently describe the Asian session's primary role as building a defined price range rather than producing large directional moves in its own right. Institutional participation from Australian, New Zealand, and Japanese markets is described as real but comparatively modest next to the European and US sessions that follow.

Multiple sources explicitly advise that a trader does not need to actively trade during the Asian session to benefit from it - the session's main value within ICT's framework is observational: the high and low it establishes become reference points (the Asian Range, covered next) used by the sessions that follow.
concepts.beginner_explanation: As one major financial center closes for the day, another one across the world is just opening. The Asian session is simply the block of hours when Japanese, Australian, and other Asia-Pacific markets are the primary active participants - generally a quieter, calmer period compared to what follows once London and then New York open.
detection_criteria: Note the approximate window (commonly cited across sources as roughly 8:00 PM to 12:00 AM Eastern Time, though some sources cite a narrower 8:00 - 10:00 PM window - see the qualification below).
Observe whether price during this window is forming a relatively narrow, contained range rather than a strong directional trend.
Refrain from expecting large, reliable directional moves during this window, consistent with ICT-focused guidance.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
Price oscillates narrowly between 100 and 103 from 8:00 PM to 12:00 AM ET, without a decisive break in either direction

This narrow, contained oscillation is typical of how ICT-focused sources describe Asian session behavior - not the absence of any movement, but movement that stays within a defined, relatively tight boundary rather than trending strongly.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
The Asian session tells the trader that a reference range is being built, information that becomes directly useful once the next concept (Asian Range) and later sessions are considered - it also sets initial expectations for muted volatility.

It does not tell the trader that no significant moves can occur during this window; occasional volatility, particularly around region-specific news, can still occur.
common_pairings: London Session (which frequently targets the Asian range)
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: The Asian session's defining contribution to the rest of the day is the range it builds - this is why it is immediately followed in this module by the Asian Range concept, and why the London session (covered later) is so frequently described in relation to it.

framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds directly into Asian Range and Asian Kill Zone.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Forcing trades during the Asian session expecting London-session-level volatility and directional movement.
Ignoring the Asian session's range entirely, missing the reference points it provides for later sessions.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: Not every day produces a clean, well-defined Asian range. Occasionally the session itself trends or remains highly erratic, particularly around scheduled economic news from Asia-Pacific economies, which limits the reliability of the range-building assumption on any single given day.

concepts.name: Asian Range
concepts.definition: The Asian Range is the specific high and low price boundary established during the Asian session, marked and carried forward as a key reference level for the trading day, since later sessions are frequently observed to move toward and through one side of this range in search of liquidity.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
ICT-focused teaching treats the Asian Range as a direct application of the liquidity concepts from Module 4: because price has generally consolidated within a defined band during the Asian session, resting buy-stop orders are presumed to accumulate just above the range high, and resting sell-stop orders just below the range low - turning the Asian Range into the day's first clearly marked buy-side and sell-side liquidity pools.

Multiple sources describe the standard first task of a trading day, under this framework, as physically marking two horizontal lines: one at the Asian session's highest point, and one at its lowest - these two lines then become the primary reference levels watched through the London session that follows.
concepts.beginner_explanation: If the Asian session is a period where price mostly moves sideways within a narrow band, the Asian Range is simply that band itself - the exact top and bottom prices reached during those quieter hours, marked so they can be watched closely once the busier London session begins.
detection_criteria: After the Asian session window has concluded (or as it develops, using its high/low so far), identify the highest price reached and the lowest price reached during that window.
Draw a horizontal line at each of these two levels.
Label the upper line as a candidate buy-side liquidity pool and the lower line as a candidate sell-side liquidity pool (Module 4).
Carry both lines forward into the subsequent London session as active reference points.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
During the Asian session, price ranges between a low of 100 and a high of 103

A trader following this method would mark two lines: one at 103 (the Asian Range high, a candidate buy-side liquidity pool) and one at 100 (the Asian Range low, a candidate sell-side liquidity pool), then watch closely for the London session's reaction to either level.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
The Asian Range tells the trader the specific price levels most likely to be targeted for a liquidity sweep once the London session begins, directly connecting Module 4's liquidity concepts to a specific, dated, and repeatable daily reference.

It does not tell the trader which side of the range will be swept first, or whether the eventual sweep will be followed by a reversal or a genuine breakout continuation - that judgment depends on the concepts covered in the London Session and London Open Kill Zone sections below.
common_pairings: Judas Swing (covered under London Open Kill Zone)
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: The Asian Range is simply a dated, specific instance of the general buy-side/sell-side liquidity concepts from Module 4, and it is the single most commonly cited setup for the Judas Swing pattern discussed under the London Open Kill Zone.

framework_placement.comes_before: Requires Asian Session and Buy-Side/Sell-Side Liquidity (Module 4).
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds directly into the London Session and London Open Kill Zone, where the range is most commonly acted upon.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Forgetting to update the Asian Range if the session is still in progress and price makes a new high or low after the range was first marked.
Treating the Asian Range as a guaranteed target rather than a probable one - some days, neither side of the range is meaningfully tested.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: The Asian Range is a probable, not guaranteed, area of interest for later sessions. A given day's price action may fail to interact meaningfully with either boundary, particularly during holidays or unusually quiet periods across all sessions.

concepts.name: Asian Kill Zone
concepts.definition: The Asian Kill Zone is a specific, narrower time window within the broader Asian session, cited across ICT-focused sources as approximately 8:00 PM to 10:00 PM or 8:00 PM to 12:00 AM Eastern Time, during which Asian-session activity and range formation are considered most relevant to watch.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
ICT-focused sources are notably inconsistent on the exact boundaries of this specific window - some cite a tight 8:00 - 10:00 PM ET range, others extend it to 8:00 PM - 12:00 AM ET, and still others frame it in GMT terms (such as 20:00 - 00:00 GMT) without a precisely matching ET conversion across all sources. This book documents this variance explicitly rather than presenting one version as the single settled definition.

Despite the disagreement on exact timing, sources are consistent on the Asian Kill Zone's purpose and character: it is generally treated as the least active of the four major Kill Zones for direct trade entries, and is instead used primarily for range-marking and observation, as described in the Asian Range concept above. A minority of sources note it can offer modest scalping opportunities specifically on Asia-Pacific currency pairs (AUD, NZD, JPY).
concepts.beginner_explanation: The Asian Kill Zone is simply a slightly more specific, narrowed-down clock-time window within the broader Asian session - the particular hours ICT-focused traders pay the closest attention to for marking the day's initial reference range, even though, as with the broader session, actual trade entries are not typically expected here.
detection_criteria: Note the current time in New York (Eastern Time).
Check whether it falls within the commonly cited Asian Kill Zone window (approximately 8:00 PM to 10:00 PM, or as late as 12:00 AM, depending on the specific source referenced).
During this window, focus on observing and marking the developing Asian Range rather than seeking entries.
Adjust for daylight saving time shifts as needed, per Time and Price Theory.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
8:00 PM - 10:00 PM ET: price consolidates from 100 to 103; no clear entries taken

A trader following ICT-focused guidance would use this window primarily to observe and mark the 100 - 103 range, rather than to place trades, reserving active decision-making for the London and New York Kill Zones covered next.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
The Asian Kill Zone tells the trader when to pay close attention for range-marking purposes, and, more cautiously, when a small number of sources suggest modest scalping opportunities may exist on specific Asia-Pacific currency pairs.

It does not tell the trader to expect the same scale or reliability of movement as the London or New York Kill Zones, and does not itself specify a precise, universally agreed clock-time boundary.
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: This Kill Zone exists specifically to support the Asian Range concept and to set up the London Open Kill Zone's most common pattern (the Judas Swing sweep of that range).

framework_placement.comes_before: Requires Asian Session and Time and Price Theory.
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into the London Session and London Open Kill Zone.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Assuming there is one single, universally agreed exact clock-time definition for this window, rather than recognizing the documented variance across sources.
Seeking aggressive entries during this window with the same expectations applied to the London or New York Kill Zones.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: This book documents a genuine, unresolved variance in exact clock-time boundaries for the Asian Kill Zone across ICT-focused secondary sources. Readers should verify the specific timing convention used by any given source, tool, or broker before relying on a precise boundary, and should treat the underlying purpose (range-marking, modest expectations) as more consistently agreed-upon than the exact minute-by-minute window.

concepts.name: London Session
concepts.definition: The London session is the trading period during which European financial centers, principally London, are active - described consistently across ICT-focused sources as the world's largest forex trading session by volume and the period most likely to establish the high or low of the entire trading day.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
ICT-focused sources are highly consistent that the London session's opening hours are the single most closely watched window in the ICT daily framework for forex traders, due to the sheer scale of institutional participation once major European bank and fund trading desks come online.

The dominant pattern associated with this session across nearly every source reviewed is the Judas Swing (detailed fully under London Open Kill Zone, next): a false initial move, typically sweeping the Asian Range in one direction, followed by a sharp reversal into what is presented as the genuine directional move of the day.
concepts.beginner_explanation: As the Asian session winds down, European markets - with London as the largest global center for currency trading - begin their business day. The London session is this period of European market activity, and ICT-focused sources treat its opening hours as unusually consequential: what happens here is described as very often deciding the overall direction and range for the entire rest of the day.
detection_criteria: Note the transition from the quieter Asian session hours into the substantially higher-volume London session hours.
Observe whether price begins moving more decisively, in either direction, compared to the narrower Asian Range.
Reference the previously marked Asian Range high and low as the specific levels most likely to be tested or swept during this session's opening hours.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
Asian range: 100 - 103. At London open, price spikes to 104 (sweeping the Asian high) before reversing sharply down to 96

This pattern - a brief spike beyond the Asian Range high, followed by a sharp reversal well below the range - is exactly the kind of price action ICT-focused sources describe as characteristic of the London session's opening hours, and is the specific pattern named and explained in detail in the next concept.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
The London session tells the trader that the probability of a significant, tradeable directional move rises substantially compared to the Asian session, and that the Asian Range is the specific reference most likely to be acted upon.

It does not tell the trader in advance which direction the eventual genuine move will take - an initial spike in one direction is frequently, according to ICT-focused sources, the opposite of the day's ultimate direction.
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: The London session's behavior is defined largely in relation to the Asian Range that precedes it and sets up much of what the New York session does afterward - ICT-focused sources describe New York as either continuing or reversing what London established.

framework_placement.comes_before: Requires Asian Session, Asian Range, and Time and Price Theory.
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds directly into London Open Kill Zone and London Close Kill Zone.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Assuming the first directional move seen at London's open is automatically the day's genuine direction, without waiting for confirmation of a sweep-and-reversal pattern.
Trading London session moves without first having marked the Asian Range as a reference.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: Not every day features a clean Judas Swing pattern at the London open; some days see a genuine breakout continuation in the direction of the initial move, without a meaningful reversal. Distinguishing the two in real time requires the specific confirmation criteria discussed in the London Open Kill Zone concept.

concepts.name: London Open Kill Zone
concepts.definition: The London Open Kill Zone is the specific time window, cited across ICT-focused sources as approximately 2:00 AM to 5:00 AM Eastern Time (with some sources citing a narrower 2:00 - 4:00 AM window), during which the London session's opening activity - most notably the Judas Swing pattern - is expected to occur.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
The centerpiece pattern associated with this window across virtually all ICT-focused sources reviewed is the Judas Swing: a named reference to the biblical betrayal, describing a deliberately misleading initial price move - typically a sweep of the Asian Range high or low - that traps breakout traders and triggers stop-loss orders before reversing sharply into what is presented as the genuine directional move of the day.

Sources describe a specific, repeatable sequence within this window: price sweeps one side of the Asian Range, this sweep is followed by displacement in the opposite direction (Module 5), which is then confirmed by a Market Structure Shift (Module 3) on a lower timeframe (commonly the 5-minute chart), typically leaving behind a Fair Value Gap used as the specific entry zone.

Multiple sources provide an explicit invalidation rule for distinguishing a genuine Judas Swing from an actual breakout: if price fails to reclaim the swept level within a small number of candles (some sources cite 2 - 3 candles on a 5-minute chart), the move is treated as a genuine breakout rather than a Judas Swing, and the reversal-based trade idea is considered invalidated.
concepts.beginner_explanation: Named after a figure who appeared to be an ally before betraying that trust, the Judas Swing is a price move that looks, at first glance, like the real direction of the day - but is actually a trap. Price pushes convincingly past the Asian session's high or low, luring in traders who assume a breakout is underway, and then reverses hard in the opposite direction. The London Open Kill Zone is the specific window where ICT-focused teaching expects this exact pattern to play out.
detection_criteria: Confirm the current time falls within the London Open Kill Zone (commonly cited as roughly 2:00 AM - 5:00 AM ET).
Reference the previously marked Asian Range high and low.
Watch for price to sweep beyond one of these two levels.
Confirm this sweep is followed by displacement in the opposite direction, and by a Market Structure Shift on a lower timeframe.
Confirm price does not reclaim the swept level within roughly 2 - 3 candles on that lower timeframe - if it does, treat the move as a genuine breakout rather than a Judas Swing.
Use the resulting Fair Value Gap, if one forms, as the specific entry zone in the new, reversed direction.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
Asian range: 100 - 103. At 2:30 AM ET, price spikes to 104.5 (sweeping BSL above 103), then reverses with displacement down through 100, confirming a bearish MSS on the 5-minute chart and leaving an FVG between 100.5 and 101.5.

This full sequence - a sweep of the Asian high, followed by displacement, a confirmed structure shift, and a resulting Fair Value Gap - is the textbook Judas Swing pattern described across ICT-focused sources. The FVG between 100.5 and 101.5 would be marked as the specific entry zone for a short position, targeting the sell-side liquidity resting below the Asian Range low near 100 and beyond.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
The London Open Kill Zone tells the trader specifically when and how the day's initial directional "trap" is expected to unfold, providing a repeatable, structured sequence (sweep, displacement, structure shift, FVG entry) rather than a vague expectation of "volatility."

It does not tell the trader, at the moment the initial spike occurs, whether that spike is definitely a Judas Swing about to reverse or a genuine breakout about to continue - this can only be confirmed using the specific invalidation criteria described above, applied after the fact.
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: This Kill Zone is the single most complete, practical illustration in this book so far of the full sweep-then-displacement-then-structure-shift sequence introduced across Modules 3 through 5, applied to a specific, named, time-bound setup.

framework_placement.comes_before: Requires Asian Range, Liquidity Sweep (Module 4), Displacement (Module 5), and Market Structure Shift (Module 3).
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds directly into London Close Kill Zone and the New York Session, which frequently continues or reverses whatever direction London established.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Entering a trade in the direction of the initial spike, assuming it is the genuine move, without waiting for a possible reversal.
Entering a reversal trade immediately upon seeing the sweep, without confirming displacement and a structure shift first.
Ignoring the invalidation rule and continuing to treat a sustained, reclaimed-level move as a Judas Swing when it has, in fact, become a genuine breakout.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: Not every trading day produces a clean Judas Swing. Sources explicitly acknowledge that the pattern can fail to appear, or that an apparent sweep can instead be the start of a genuine breakout - the specific invalidation criteria exist precisely because this distinction cannot be made with certainty until after the fact.

concepts.name: London Close Kill Zone
concepts.definition: The London Close Kill Zone is the specific time window, cited across ICT-focused sources as approximately 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM Eastern Time (with some sources citing a narrower 8:00 - 9:00 AM window), during which European trading desks finalize and close out positions ahead of the London session's end, often producing continuation or corrective price behavior that extends into the New York afternoon.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
ICT-focused sources consistently describe this window as more subtle and lower-probability than the London Open or New York Open Kill Zones, but still worth monitoring, particularly for continuation setups extending moves that began earlier in the London or New York sessions.

One specifically documented pattern associated with this window is a counter-trend retracement: after price has extended strongly in one direction through the London and early New York sessions, a liquidity raid of the session's high or low, followed by a shift back toward the day's opening price, is described as a lower-probability but still notable setup, typically traded with reduced position size relative to the day's primary setups.
concepts.beginner_explanation: As the London trading day winds down, European desks are described as closing out or adjusting their positions before finishing for the day. The London Close Kill Zone is this specific window - generally quieter and less dramatic than the London or New York opens, but still capable of producing meaningful, if smaller, price moves as that final adjustment happens.
detection_criteria: Confirm the current time falls within the commonly cited London Close Kill Zone window.
Assess whether price has already extended meaningfully in one direction during the earlier London and New York sessions.
Watch for a liquidity raid of the day's established high or low, followed by a retracement back toward the day's opening price.
Treat any resulting setup with reduced size/confidence relative to the day's primary London Open or New York Open setups.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
After a strong bullish move earlier in the day (100 → 120), price spikes to 122 (a liquidity raid of the day's high) around 10:30 AM ET, then retraces back toward 110 (the day's opening price)

This late-session raid-and-retrace pattern is the type of counter-trend setup ICT-focused sources associate with the London Close Kill Zone - a smaller, corrective move rather than a fresh, primary directional push.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
The London Close Kill Zone tells the trader when to expect a final, smaller wave of directional adjustment or correction as the European trading day winds down, and gives a specific, named context (rather than "random afternoon movement") for interpreting that behavior.

It does not tell the trader to expect the same scale or reliability as the day's primary Kill Zones, and ICT-focused sources are explicit in describing this as a lower-probability window warranting smaller position sizing.
common_pairings: Fair Value Gap (Module 5, for the counter-move entry)
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: This window is best understood as a coda to the day's primary London Open and New York Open activity, and its specific trade setup (a counter-trend retracement into a Fair Value Gap formed by the counter-move) directly reuses Module 5's Fair Value Gap concept.

framework_placement.comes_before: Requires London Session, London Open Kill Zone, and Fair Value Gap (Module 5).
framework_placement.comes_after: Feeds into the New York Session and Session-to-Session Relationships, the module's final concept.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Treating a London Close Kill Zone setup with the same confidence and position sizing as a London Open or New York Open setup.
Ignoring this window entirely and missing legitimate, if smaller, continuation or corrective opportunities it can present.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: This is explicitly described across sources as the lowest-probability of the named Kill Zones. As with the Asian Kill Zone, exact clock-time boundaries vary somewhat across sources, and this window's setups should be treated with appropriately reduced confidence and size.

concepts.name: New York Session
concepts.definition: The New York session is the trading period during which US financial markets are active, described across ICT-focused sources as producing the highest overall trading volume of the day (particularly during its overlap with the tail end of the London session) and as either continuing or reversing whatever directional move the London session established.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
ICT-focused sources are consistent that reading the New York session correctly requires first understanding what happened during the London session - the central analytical question posed across multiple sources is not simply "what is price doing now," but "what did Asia build, and what did London already do to it?"

The New York session's opening hours specifically overlap with major scheduled US economic data releases (commonly cited as occurring around 8:30 AM ET) and the US equity market open (9:30 AM ET), both of which are described as contributing to this session's high overall volume and its potential for sharp, news-driven displacement.
concepts.beginner_explanation: As the European trading day winds down, US markets are just beginning theirs. The New York session is this period of US market activity, and ICT-focused teaching treats it as the day's final, and often decisive, chapter - either confirming and extending the story London already started, or overturning it entirely.
detection_criteria: Confirm the transition from the London session into New York session hours, generally marked by rising volume as US market participants become active.
Review what direction, if any, the London session established, and where it left the Asian Range's liquidity levels.
Watch New York's early price action for signs of continuing London's direction versus reversing it.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
London session trended from 100 to 96 (bearish). New York opens and price continues falling to 90.

This is an example of New York session continuation: rather than reversing the bearish move London established, the New York session extends it further in the same direction - one of the two general outcomes ICT-focused sources describe for this session.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
The New York session tells the trader whether the prior session's directional story is being confirmed or overturned, and provides the day's highest-volume window for potential displacement, particularly around scheduled economic data releases.

It does not tell the trader in advance which of the two outcomes (continuation or reversal) will occur - this must be judged from actual price behavior once the session begins, using the structure and liquidity tools from earlier modules.
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: The New York session's behavior is defined specifically in relation to the London session that precedes it, and together the two (plus the Asian session before them) form the full daily cycle formalized in the next module's Power of 3 framework.

beginner_mistakes_or_misinterpretations: Analyzing New York session price action without first reviewing what happened during the Asian and London sessions earlier that day.
Assuming New York will always continue London's direction, when reversal is an equally documented, common outcome.
concepts.qualification_or_limits: Whether New York continues or reverses London's move cannot be predicted with certainty in advance; ICT-focused sources describe both outcomes as common, with the correct read depending on the specific structural and liquidity evidence present at the time, not on a fixed rule about which session "usually" wins.

concepts.name: New York Open Kill Zone
concepts.definition: The New York Open Kill Zone is the specific time window, cited across ICT-focused sources with meaningful variation as approximately 7:00 - 10:00 AM, 8:00 - 11:00 AM, or 8:30 - 11:00 AM Eastern Time, during which the overlap of late London activity, major US economic data releases, and the US equity market open combine to produce the day's highest-volume trading conditions.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
Sources are consistent in describing this as one of the two most important Kill Zones of the day (alongside the London Open), but disagree meaningfully on its precise start and end times - some anchor it to forex-specific hours (7:00 - 10:00 AM ET), others to a window bracketing the 8:30 AM ET economic data releases (8:00 - 11:00 AM or 8:30 - 11:00 AM ET), and still others to the 9:30 AM ET equity market open specifically. As with the Asian Kill Zone, this book documents this variance explicitly.

A specific, narrower sub-window within this Kill Zone, referenced across several sources by name, is the "Silver Bullet" - commonly cited as 10:00 - 11:00 AM ET - described as a further-refined setup window within the broader New York Open Kill Zone, though this book does not treat the Silver Bullet as a separately numbered concept, since it falls outside the specific concept list this module is built around.

The dominant expected pattern here, according to multiple sources, mirrors the London Open: a liquidity sweep (often of the Asian Range, the London session's high/low, or the prior day's high/low) followed by displacement and a structure shift, frequently coinciding with the 8:30 AM ET economic news release.
concepts.beginner_explanation: The New York Open Kill Zone is the specific stretch of the morning, US Eastern Time, when several major events are all happening close together: European markets are just finishing their day, big US economic reports are coming out, and the US stock market is opening. ICT-focused teaching treats this pile-up of activity as the day's single busiest, most consequential window for price action.
detection_criteria: Confirm the current time falls within the New York Open Kill Zone (being aware that different sources cite somewhat different specific boundaries within roughly 7:00 AM - 11:00 AM ET).
Note whether a scheduled US economic data release (commonly around 8:30 AM ET) is imminent or has just occurred.
Watch for a liquidity sweep of a relevant reference level (the Asian Range, the London high/low, or the prior day's high/low).
Confirm this sweep with displacement and a structure shift, as in the London Open Kill Zone sequence.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
London session high at 108. At 8:30 AM ET, a news release spikes price to 110 (sweeping the London high), then reverses sharply down through 105 with strong displacement.

This sequence - a news-driven spike sweeping a relevant liquidity level, followed by a sharp reversal - is the pattern ICT-focused sources most commonly associate with the New York Open Kill Zone, directly paralleling the London Open Kill Zone's Judas Swing but keyed to the New York morning's specific liquidity events.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
The New York Open Kill Zone tells the trader when the day's highest-volume, and often highest-volatility, window is expected, and provides a specific, repeatable pattern (news-driven sweep, displacement, structure shift) to watch for within it.

It does not tell the trader the exact minute this activity will occur, nor does it guarantee the news release itself will produce a clean, tradable sequence rather than simply erratic, directionless volatility.
concepts.common_pairings_narrative: This Kill Zone reuses the exact same sweep-displacement-structure-shift sequence taught under the London Open Kill Zone, applied to New York's specific liquidity references and news calendar.

concepts.qualification_or_limits: As with the Asian and London Close Kill Zones, this book documents a genuine, unresolved variance in exact clock-time boundaries for the New York Open Kill Zone across ICT-focused secondary sources. The underlying pattern (news-adjacent liquidity sweep, displacement, structure shift) is more consistently agreed upon than the precise minute-by-minute window.

concepts.name: How to Use Each Session
concepts.definition: This concept consolidates the practical, role-based guidance from the individual session and Kill Zone concepts above into a single applied framework: what a trader should actually do - observe, mark, watch, or act - during each of the four named windows.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
ICT-focused teaching assigns each session a distinct functional role rather than treating all four as equally suited to the same activity: the Asian session/Kill Zone for range-marking and observation; the London Open Kill Zone for the day's primary directional setup (via the Judas Swing sequence); the London Close Kill Zone for smaller, lower-confidence continuation or corrective setups; and the New York Open Kill Zone for either the day's primary setup (if London's Judas Swing did not clearly resolve) or a continuation/confirmation of what London already established.

A recurring piece of guidance across sources is that a trader does not need to actively trade every session, or even most of them - observing and marking reference levels during quieter windows (Asia, London Close) while reserving actual entries for the highest-probability windows (London Open, New York Open) is described as a more disciplined and sustainable approach than attempting to trade continuously around the clock.
concepts.beginner_explanation: Having learned what each individual session and Kill Zone tends to look like, this concept is simply the practical summary: what should you actually be doing with your attention during each one? The short version, repeated across ICT-focused sources, is watch and mark during the quiet Asian hours, look for the main event during the London open, treat the London close gently, and treat the New York open as either the main event (if London didn't deliver) or the confirmation of what London already did.
detection_criteria: During the Asian session/Kill Zone: mark the range high and low; avoid expecting large directional trades.
During the London Open Kill Zone: watch closely for a Judas Swing sweep of the Asian Range, followed by displacement and a structure shift; this is generally the day's primary setup opportunity.
During the London Close Kill Zone: watch for smaller, lower-confidence continuation or corrective setups; size any resulting trades conservatively.

During the New York Open Kill Zone: assess whether London already delivered a clear directional move; if so, watch for continuation; if not, treat this window as the day's primary setup opportunity instead.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
Asia: range 100 - 103 (observed only). London Open: Judas Swing sweeps 103, reverses to 95 with MSS and FVG (primary trade taken here). New York Open: price continues falling to 90 (continuation, smaller add-on trade considered).

This walk-through illustrates the role-based approach: no trade during Asia, the primary trade during London Open (where the full confirmed sequence appeared), and a smaller continuation consideration during New York Open, rather than treating every session identically.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
This concept tells the trader how to allocate attention and risk differently across the trading day, rather than treating every hour as equally worth watching or trading.

It does not tell the trader that this exact role assignment will play out identically every single day - some days the primary setup occurs at New York Open instead of London Open, particularly when London's session is unusually quiet or indecisive.

concepts.name: Session-to-Session Relationships
concepts.definition: Session-to-session relationships describe the dependency chain ICT-focused teaching identifies running through the trading day: the Asian session builds a range, the London session acts on that range (typically via a Judas Swing), and the New York session either continues or reverses whatever direction London established - each session's behavior is read in light of what the prior session already did, not in isolation.
concepts.ict_specific_meaning:
This concept is the explicit statement of a theme implicit throughout this entire module: sources consistently frame the correct analytical question during any given session as being about the prior session's behavior, not just the current session's price action in isolation. One source phrases this directly as: the relevant question is rarely "what is price doing now," but "what did the earlier session build, and what has the current session already done to it?"

This chain of dependency is described as the daily-cycle version of a fractal pattern that recurs at other scales within ICT-focused teaching (for example, the same accumulation-then-manipulation-then-distribution logic that Module 9's Power of 3 formalizes as a repeatable template, and that some sources describe as applying at the weekly level as well as the daily level).
concepts.beginner_explanation: No single session exists in a vacuum. What Asia does sets the stage for London's opening move; what London does (especially whether it delivers a clean Judas Swing or not) sets the stage for how the New York session is likely to be read. Understanding today's price action, under this framework, means understanding the whole day's story so far - not just glancing at the current five minutes of the chart.
detection_criteria: Before analyzing any session's price action, review what the immediately preceding session(s) established - specifically their range, any liquidity swept, and any resulting displacement or structure shift.
Frame the current session's price action explicitly in relation to that prior context (continuation, reversal, or as-yet-undetermined).
Update this running narrative as each new session unfolds, rather than treating each session as a fresh, unconnected start.
concepts.numeric_or_narrative_example:
Asia: range 100 - 103. London: sweeps 103, reverses to 95 (bearish MSS, FVG left at 97 - 99). New York: opens near 95, sweeps down to 93 (taking out a minor prior low), then reverses back up through 99 and continues to 108.

Read in isolation, the New York session's initial dip to 93 might look like simple bearish continuation. Read in the context of the full day's narrative - Asia built a range, London already delivered its bearish Judas Swing and structure shift - the New York dip to 93 is more plausibly interpreted as a final liquidity grab before a larger reversal back to the day's actual bullish resolution at 108, a conclusion only available by tracing the full session-to-session chain rather than viewing New York's price action alone.
concepts.what_it_tells_the_trader:
Session-to-session relationships tell the trader to maintain a continuously updated narrative across the trading day, rather than resetting their analysis from scratch at the start of every new session.

It does not tell the trader that this narrative is ever fully certain in real time - each session's true role in the day's story (setup, confirmation, or reversal) is often only clear in hindsight, once the full day has played out.

Each day's specific chain of events must be read from that day's actual price action, not assumed from a fixed template applied mechanically.

rules.exceptions_or_qualifiers: Genuine, unresolved variance in exact clock-time boundaries across ICT-focused secondary sources; underlying purpose (range-marking, modest expectations) more consistently agreed upon than exact window.

rules.statement: London Open Kill Zone: approximately 2:00 AM to 5:00 AM Eastern Time (some sources cite a narrower 2:00-4:00 AM window). Expected window for the Judas Swing pattern.
rules.exceptions_or_qualifiers: unspecified single canonical boundary; variance documented across sources.

rules.statement: London Close Kill Zone: approximately 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM Eastern Time (some sources cite a narrower 8:00-9:00 AM window). Lowest-probability of the named Kill Zones; treat setups with reduced size/confidence.

rules.exceptions_or_qualifiers: Genuine, unresolved variance across sources; underlying pattern (news-adjacent liquidity sweep, displacement, structure shift) more consistently agreed upon than the precise window.

rules.statement: All Kill Zone boundaries are anchored to New York (Eastern Time), regardless of the trader's own physical location, and shift by one hour whenever the US or UK individually transitions between standard and daylight saving time, since the two do not always change on the same calendar date.

relationships.statement:
This module follows the literal chronology of a trading day. Time and Price Theory is the foundational justification for treating time as a meaningful variable at all. Asian Session, Asian Range, and Asian Kill Zone describe the day's opening chapter: a period of consolidation that leaves behind two specific, markable reference levels. London Session, London Open Kill Zone, and London Close Kill Zone describe the day's most consequential chapter for most instruments - anchored by the Judas Swing, a direct, practical, fully worked application of the liquidity-sweep-then-displacement-then-structure-shift sequence built up across Modules 3 through 5.

New York Session and New York Open Kill Zone describe the day's final chapter, read specifically in relation to what the earlier sessions already established. How to Use Each Session consolidates all of this into practical guidance - not every window deserves the same attention or the same trading behavior. Session-to-Session Relationships closes the module by making explicit the thread running through everything in it: each session's price action is only fully legible in light of the sessions that came before it, a running narrative rather than a series of disconnected snapshots.

no_trade_conditions.statement: Some days offer no clean setup in any session; disciplined inaction is treated as a legitimate, expected outcome, not a failure.
During the Asian session/Kill Zone: avoid expecting large directional trades; mark the range only, do not seek entries.

contradictions_or_ambiguities.description: Exact clock-time boundaries for every named Kill Zone (Asian, London Open, London Close, New York Open) vary across ICT-focused secondary sources, sometimes by one to three hours on a given boundary. The book documents this explicitly rather than presenting a single false consensus.

passage_a.text: A note on sourcing for this specific module: exact clock-time boundaries for each named Kill Zone vary meaningfully across ICT-focused secondary sources - sometimes by one to three hours on a given boundary.

passage_b.text: unspecified - variance is documented individually within each Kill Zone concept rather than as a single conflicting pair of passages.

contradictions_or_ambiguities.description: London Close Kill Zone timing shows a particularly stark discrepancy: cited as approximately 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM ET by some sources but as narrow as 8:00-9:00 AM ET by others -- these windows do not overlap at all, unlike the milder 1-3 hour variances seen for other Kill Zones.

passage_a.text: The London Close Kill Zone is the specific time window, cited across ICT-focused sources as approximately 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM Eastern Time (with some sources citing a narrower 8:00-9:00 AM window)...

passage_b.text: unspecified - no reconciliation of the two non-overlapping windows is offered in the text.

module_review_notes.beginner_summary: ICT-focused teaching treats the trading day as unevenly weighted: specific windows tied to the opening of major financial centers - Asia/Tokyo, London, and New York - are treated as far more likely to contain significant, tradeable price action than the hours in between. The Asian session typically builds a defined range, whose high and low become the day's first liquidity reference points. The London session's opening hours are the single most closely watched window for most instruments, characterized by the Judas Swing: a false initial move that sweeps the Asian Range before reversing sharply into the day's genuine direction, confirmed by displacement and a structure shift. The London Close is a quieter, lower-confidence window for continuation or corrective moves. The New York session, particularly its opening hours (which overlap with major US economic data and the equity market open), either continues or reverses whatever London already established - and reading it correctly requires understanding the full story of the day so far, not just the current session in isolation.
module_review_notes.concept_relationships_summary: Time and Price Theory is the foundational justification for the entire module. Asian Session, Asian Range, and Asian Kill Zone form the day's first chapter. London Session, London Open Kill Zone, and London Close Kill Zone form the day's most consequential chapter. New York Session and New York Open Kill Zone form the day's final chapter, read in relation to what came before. How to Use Each Session and Session-to-Session Relationships consolidate the whole module into practical, narrative-aware guidance.
module_review_notes.practical_chart_exercise: Using the following simplified single-day sequence - Asian session: range 50 - 54; London Open (2:30 AM ET): spike to 55.5 (sweeping the Asian high), then reversal with displacement down through 49, confirming a bearish MSS and leaving an FVG at 49.5 - 50.5; New York Open (8:30 AM ET): price dips to 47 before reversing back up through 52 and continuing to 60 - identify which specific session/Kill Zone each event belongs to, state whether the New York session's initial dip to 47 should be read as bearish continuation or as a final liquidity grab before a larger reversal, and explain your reasoning using the session-to-session narrative approach from this module.
self_test_questions: Why does ICT-focused teaching treat certain hours of the day as more significant than others, rather than treating the 24-hour trading day as uniform?
What is the Asian Range, and why do its high and low become important reference points for the sessions that follow?
Describe, in order, the four steps of a full Judas Swing sequence.
What specific rule helps distinguish a genuine Judas Swing from an actual breakout?
Why does this module argue that New York session price action should not be analyzed in isolation from the Asian and London sessions earlier that same day?
common_misconceptions: Believing there is one single, universally agreed exact clock-time definition for each Kill Zone, rather than recognizing the documented variance across ICT-focused sources.
Assuming the first directional move at any session's open is automatically the day's genuine direction, without waiting for possible reversal confirmation.
Believing every session is equally suited to active trade entries, rather than understanding that some (Asian, London Close) are primarily for observation or lower-confidence, smaller setups.
Analyzing a session's price action without first reviewing what the prior session(s) already established that same day.
